Theological Liberalism
thee-uh-LOJ-i-kul LIB-er-uh-liz-um
noun phrase (movement)
Modern Protestant movement originating in late-18th-century Germany (Schleiermacher, Lessing) and reaching full institutional dominance in the early-20th-century American mainline churches. The term "liberal" carries the post-Enlightenment sense of "free from constraint by traditional authority," not the contemporary American political sense.

📖 Biblical Definition

Theological liberalism is the modern Protestant movement that revises historic Christian doctrine to make it compatible with post-Enlightenment naturalism, modern science, and modern moral sensibility. Originating with Friedrich Schleiermacher (On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers, 1799; The Christian Faith, 1821-22), developed by Albrecht Ritschl, Adolf von Harnack (What Is Christianity?, 1900), and Walter Rauschenbusch (Social Gospel), it reached full institutional dominance in the American mainline Protestant churches by roughly 1920-1930 and provoked the great fundamentalist-modernist controversy of the 1920s. Its defining moves: doctrine is reduced to ethics or to religious feeling; miracles are denied or reinterpreted naturalistically; the deity of Christ is denied or recast (Christ as the supreme religious teacher rather than the eternal Son incarnate); substitutionary atonement is replaced by exemplarist or moral-influence theories; biblical inerrancy is denied; the historic creeds are revised or abandoned. J. Gresham Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923) made the decisive Reformed-confessional argument: liberalism is not a variant of Christianity but a different religion that uses Christian vocabulary. The dictionary holds Machen's verdict. The 20th-century American mainline Protestant decline (the so-called "empty mainline pews") is the empirical confirmation of Machen's diagnosis. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts theological liberalism by name.

THEOLOGICAL LIBERALISM, noun phrase. Modern Protestant movement, late 18th century onward.

Founders: Friedrich Schleiermacher (German; On Religion, 1799; The Christian Faith, 1821-22).

Major representatives: Albrecht Ritschl; Adolf von Harnack (What Is Christianity?, 1900); Walter Rauschenbusch (Social Gospel); Harry Emerson Fosdick.

Dominant in American mainline Protestant churches by 1920-1930; provoked fundamentalist-modernist controversy of 1920s; reorganized as "Neo-Orthodoxy" (Barth, Brunner, Niebuhr) mid-century.

Decisive Reformed-confessional rebuttal: J. Gresham Machen, Christianity and Liberalism (1923) — liberalism is not a variant of Christianity but a different religion.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Theological liberalism is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry exists to identify the movement's founders, document its defining moves, and rebut it via Machen's 1923 verdict and the empirical 20th-century mainline decline.

expand to see more

Christian vocabulary, different religion. Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923) made the decisive argument: liberalism uses words like God, Christ, salvation, gospel, atonement, and Bible, but its content for each word is so different from historic Christianity's content that it constitutes a different religion. Liberalism's God is immanent rather than transcendent-and-immanent; its Christ is the supreme moral example rather than the eternal Son incarnate; its salvation is moral self-improvement under divine encouragement rather than imputed righteousness through faith alone; its gospel is the brotherhood of humanity under the fatherhood of God; its atonement is moral influence; its Bible is the religious testimony of an evolving community. Each of these is the substitution of a modern philosophical content for the historic Christian content of the same word.

Mainline decline as empirical confirmation. The 20th-century American mainline Protestant decline is the empirical history of liberalism's diagnosis. The mainline denominations that embraced theological liberalism most fully (PCUSA, ECUSA, UMC, ELCA, DOC) have hemorrhaged membership for roughly seventy years, while confessionally conservative Reformed-evangelical communions (PCA, OPC, SBC pre-2020, EPC, ARP) have either grown or held steady. The pattern is so consistent that secular sociologists of religion have made it a textbook case. Empirical confirmation of Machen's 1923 prediction: a movement that surrenders the doctrinal substance of historic Christianity cannot sustain itself for long, because the doctrinal substance is precisely what the gospel is.
